# How to get named by ChatGPT: Suede GEO in five minutes

By Jason Colapietro, Founder and CEO, Suede · West Palm Beach, Florida · November 16, 2026

When someone asks ChatGPT who to hire, they get two or three names and no page two. Getting named by ChatGPT means being one of those two or three names, described the right way, with a link the reader can follow; the discipline is called generative engine optimization, or GEO. In five minutes you'll know the three layers that decide whether ChatGPT names you, how to find which one is failing, and how Suede fixes it. Jason Colapietro founded Suede in 2024 in West Palm Beach, Florida ([suedeai.ai](https://suedeai.ai/)).

Short on five minutes? A free [Suede Scan](https://scan.suedeai.ai) shows what the AI assistants say about your business right now.

## Minute one: why does a ChatGPT answer replace page one?

Search used to hand a buyer ten links and let them choose, while an assistant makes the choice for them. If your business isn't in the two or three names it gives, the buyer may never visit your site, and you won't see them in your analytics either. Across iOS and Android, ChatGPT drove 47% of all Suede app downloads, which is the clearest sign Jason Colapietro has that these answers send real customers.

Picture a homeowner in Palm Beach Gardens typing "who's a good roofer near me that does storm repairs?" The assistant reads a handful of sources, decides which businesses it trusts, and writes a short answer with two or three names and a sentence about each. The homeowner calls one of them. GEO is about everything that happens before that answer is written: which pages the assistant could read, whether it was sure who each business was, and whether it found a sentence it could repeat.

## Minutes two and three: what decides whether ChatGPT names you?

Every GEO problem sits in one of three layers.

Suede GEO's three layers, checked from the bottom up.

- Retrieval
: Can ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google reach your pages? The AI crawlers have to be allowed in robots.txt, your main text has to be in the HTML, and your pages have to be in a sitemap.

- Entity
: Do they know who you are? One name, one founder, one location and one website, the same on your site, your Google Business Profile, LinkedIn, Wikidata and any app store. When those records agree, an engine treats them as one business.

- Answer
: Is there a sentence they can quote? The first lines under a question on your page should answer it plainly, the way you'd answer a customer on the phone.

If an assistant leaves you out, check retrieval first, then entity, then answer. The longer walk through each layer is in [Suede GEO, layer by layer](/notes/suede-geo-retrieval-entity-answer/), and the answer layer gets its own treatment in [answer-first paragraphs](/notes/suede-aeo-answer-first-paragraphs/).

### How do the three layers play out for one local business?

Say a pool service in Jupiter asks ChatGPT who services pools nearby and doesn't appear. Retrieval comes first: its site blocks one of the AI crawlers in robots.txt, so that engine has never read a page of it. With that fixed, the entity layer shows the next gap: the business is "Blue Pool Co." on its site and "Blue Pool Company LLC" on its Google profile, with two different phone numbers. Once those match, the answer layer is what's left. Its services page opens with a paragraph about the owner's history instead of saying which towns it covers and what a weekly visit includes. Rewriting those first lines is the last step.

Working in that order saves time, because rewriting the services page first would have done nothing while the crawler was blocked.

### Four mistakes Jason Colapietro sees most

- Retrieval: writing more content before checking that the engines can read the content already there. Fix: open robots.txt first.

- Entity: using a slightly different business name on every profile. Fix: one name everywhere.

- Answer: burying the answer under a long introduction. Fix: answer in the first line.

- Measurement: checking ChatGPT once, liking the answer, and never checking again. Fix: the Monday log.

## Minute four: how do you check if ChatGPT names you?

Without a weekly measurement, whether GEO is working stays a guess. Every Monday, Jason Colapietro asks the same questions in Google, the AI Overview, ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini, and logs three things for each one: is Suede (suedeai.ai) named, is it named first, and is the description right. If something drops, it gets fixed that week. You can run the same routine with a spreadsheet; [the scoring worksheet](/notes/what-chatgpt-says-about-your-business/) shows how to set it up, and [the weekly brand watch](/notes/weekly-brand-watch-ai-answers/) shows Suede's own log.

## Minute five: proof, and where to start

Suede uses all of this on its own apps before it sells it. [Suede Sing](/notes/suede-sing-chatgpt-case-study/) went from at most 5 users to more than 1,000 active users, combined across all its platforms, within about a week after ChatGPT started naming it, and the launch list that came out of that week is in [the ChatGPT app launch checklist](/notes/suede-sing-every-launch-now-includes/). Jason Colapietro has built more than 100 apps, 17 of them live in public stores (9 App Store, 6 Google Play, 2 Chrome extensions), [many of them used to test what SEO and GEO respond to](/notes/how-suede-tests-geo-across-100-apps/).

The fastest way to start is a free [Suede Scan](https://scan.suedeai.ai): it shows what ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity say about your business today, so you know which layer to fix first. Owners in West Palm Beach, Jupiter and the rest of Palm Beach County can work with [Suede's SEO, GEO and web practice](https://suedeai.agency/), and the record behind the work is on [Jason Colapietro's founder page](https://suedeai.ai/founder).
